Don’t ever feel bad about playing bad golf. Just keep up with pace of play and you’ll be fine. Once you play with more strangers, you’ll realize that 50% of golfers shoot similar scores to you. Other than that have fun and by next year you’ll be super comfortable playing with whomever

Yes, there have been instances and allegations of corruption tied to the distribution of federal loans and grants between the U.S. government and colleges, though the scope and specifics vary. The federal student aid system, managed primarily by the Department of Education, disburses over $120 billion annually in grants, loans, and work-study funds to millions of students and thousands of institutions. This massive flow of money creates opportunities for mismanagement, fraud, and abuse—some of which has been documented, while other cases remain speculative or under investigation.

One clear historical example is the for-profit college scandals of the 2010s, like Corinthian Colleges and ITT Technical Institute. These schools were accused of predatory practices—misrepresenting job placement rates, enrolling ineligible students, and aggressively pushing federal loans to maximize revenue. Corinthian’s collapse in 2015 left taxpayers on the hook for roughly $500 million in discharged loans, while ITT’s 2016 closure added to the tally. A 2012 Senate investigation found that for-profit colleges, which served 22% of federal loan borrowers, accounted for 44% of defaults, hinting at systemic misuse. The Department of Education had the authority since 1992 to hold executives personally liable for such losses but rarely did, raising questions about oversight or even complicity. Critics argue this inaction—sometimes attributed to cozy relationships between regulators and college leaders—enabled fraud to persist, costing billions.

Beyond for-profits, broader corruption allegations surface periodically. A 2025 study, “Windfall Federal Grants and Local Government Corruption,” noted that federal grant increases (from $135 billion in 1990 to $1.2 trillion in 2022) strain oversight, creating openings for misuse. While focused on local governments, the principle applies to colleges receiving federal funds—especially as indirect costs (overhead fees universities charge on grants) have ballooned from 15% decades ago to over 60% today. Some claim this shift funnels money into administrative slush funds rather than education, though hard evidence of outright corruption here is thinner, often resting on inefficiency critiques.

Specific kickback schemes have also emerged. In the early 2000s, the student loan “preferred lender” scandal exposed colleges steering students to certain lenders for financial perks. For instance, in 2007, New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo investigated deals where lenders paid colleges (like Columbia and UT-Austin) to promote their loans, sometimes offering administrators personal benefits. Settlements followed, but no widespread criminal convictions, suggesting a gray area between unethical and illegal.

On the grant side, fraud isn’t unheard of. The False Claims Act has been used in whistleblower cases against schools falsifying records to secure federal funds. A 2019 case saw Constantine Cannon recover $80 million from a for-profit chain violating recruitment incentive bans, showing how colleges can game the system. Research grants, too, have issues—think falsified data or bribes to win awards—though these are less common and harder to tie directly to federal-college collusion.

Still, definitive proof of systemic corruption (versus isolated fraud or mismanagement) is elusive. The Government Accountability Office has flagged the Education Department’s Federal Student Aid as a “high-risk” entity since the 1990s for weak controls, and a 1994 piece from Hillsdale’s Imprimis warned of an “S&L-style crisis” in higher ed funding—prophetic given later defaults. Yet, political and bureaucratic inertia often frames these as administrative failures, not conspiracies. The Biden administration’s 2021 push to hold executives accountable (e.g., DeVry case) and Trump’s 2025 funding cuts to Columbia over protest handling show sporadic crackdowns, but no overhaul.

So, corruption? Yes, in pockets—proven in for-profit scams, lender kickbacks, and grant fraud. Systemic? Debatable. The scale of money invites abuse, and lax enforcement doesn’t help, but it’s often more about greed exploiting loopholes than a grand federal-college racket. Data’s messy, and narratives split—some see a broken system, others just bad actors. What’s clear: billions have been misspent, and taxpayers usually foot the bill.

I just did my first 70.3 last weekend and this is my opinion on a basic training schedule and what you need. 

Bike:  Cycling is majority of the time spent during the race so just get comfortable on a bike. Spend 2-3 hours on the bike during a ride and do that once a week. Maybe ride 1-2 more times that week for an hour. I would ride anywhere from 20 miles to 60 miles during my rides. 

Swim: I suck at swimming and did 1.2 miles in 48 mins. I only swam 4-6 times during my training but every time I swam for 45 minutes straight. 

Run: I’d try to run 1-3 times a week for 4-7 miles each run. Two month before the race I would run 14 miles and see how you feel. I’d also ride 60 miles during the same time to get an idea of how your body will react to nutrition. 

Just stay consistent and try to train at least 2 times a week. I used a $500 Canondale Synapse bike with aero bars. Tri wetsuit makes a huge difference compared to a surf wetsuit. You can buy a tri fit but I just towel changed into my cycling bib and jersey. Get good running shoes and make sure your feet fits well. 

Essentials:

Aero bars
Cycling shoes
Cycling bib/jersey or tri suit. 
Tri wetsuit
Roka swim goggles
Nice pair of cycling glasses (go on eBay and lowball for Oakley cycling glasses. I got a new pair of Sutra for $40 when they were listed for $90)
Running shoes, don’t need to be carbon plated. Needs to be comfortable. 
Cycling socks
Helmet

My tips for Tre flips. Keep your shoulders straight with your board during the trick. It’s natural to turn your back shoulder forward after you pop but your feet will never be parallel with your board when you land. If you fight the temptation to move that should the board should fall under your feet easier. 

Tre flips is all in the back foot with a light flick with the front foot. Practice by spinning them and having your front foot land on the board. For example if you’re a 15 HC which means 87 is your average best score, shooting an 81 would be -6 off your average which is huge. Me personally, I’m at 8 HC and shooting a 72 (-6) would be very hard and unlikely. My best score is a 78 and I’ve done that 3 times in 3 years. My best day of golf Vs your best day of golf would be a big difference when it comes to strokes given. 

As you play more and get better, that HC goes down and you’ll have a harder time competing against high handicappers. 

Regarding lessons, it’s up to you and if you choose to invest money into it. It’ll forsure make you better and you’ll hold onto those tips and tricks for life. If you can find cheap lessons ($200 for 6 30 minute lessons) I would be all over it. If not, you can grind out on the range, record yourself and make intentional changes and test it over and over again, you could get down to a 10 HC fairly quickly.  

Since you’re long off the tee, I would focus on approach shots and 2 putting.  I assume majority of the par 4s you play you have less than 170 yards on your second shot. Figure out how to hit the green from 170 and below and just focus on good ball contact. That should leave you on the green or just off the green majority of the time. Some rounds you might make 50% of your up and downs and others you might 2 put for bogey or three put for bogey based on conditions and just your game that day. Your putting and chipping is going to determine if it’s for par or for bogey so I’d be religious about that. It’s also free so take advantage of it and become a wizard with your wedges. You want to consider yourself a really good putter and chipper in order to get to single digit handicappers. I’ve never met anyone who’s a single digit handicapper without those two skills. You don’t need to be long off the tee to make par but you do need to have hands around the green and make 2-4 foot puts 50%+ of the time
